entry.gloss: triad with a seventh above the root
entry.def: A four-note chord: a triad with another third stacked on top, so that its notes span a seventh from the root. The five common types are named by their triad and seventh: major seventh, major-minor (dominant) seventh, minor seventh, half-diminished seventh and diminished seventh.

entry.gloss: major triad plus a major seventh
entry.def: A seventh chord made of a major triad and a major seventh above the root: C–E–G–B. In a major key it is built on the first and fourth degrees (IM7 and IVM7). Also called a major-major seventh chord; jazz writes it Cmaj7 or CΔ7.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4 B4]/h{IM7} [F4 A4 C5 E5]/h{IVM7}
figure.caption: The major seventh chords of C major.

entry.gloss: major triad plus a minor seventh
entry.def: A seventh chord made of a major triad and a minor seventh above the root, the quality of the chord on the dominant, V7: G–B–D–F in C major and minor. By quality it is a major-minor seventh chord. Its tritone between the leading tone and the seventh pulls strongly to the tonic.

entry.gloss: minor triad plus a minor seventh
entry.def: A seventh chord made of a minor triad and a minor seventh above the root: D–F–A–C. In a major key it is built on the second, third and sixth degrees (ii7, iii7, vi7). Also called a minor-minor seventh chord.

figure.staff: [D4 F4 A4 C5]/h{ii7} [A4 C5 E5 G5]/h{vi7}

entry.gloss: diminished triad plus a minor seventh
entry.def: A seventh chord made of a diminished triad and a minor seventh above the root, written with a slashed circle, ø7: B–D–F–A, viiø7 in C major, or D–F–Ab–C, iiø7 in C minor. Jazz calls it a minor seventh flat five, m7♭5.

figure.staff: [B4 D5 F5 A5]/h{viiø7} [D4 F4 Ab4 C5]/h{iiø7}
figure.caption: viiø7 in C major and iiø7 in C minor.

entry.gloss: diminished triad plus a diminished seventh
entry.def: A seventh chord made of a diminished triad and a diminished seventh above the root, so it is three stacked minor thirds: G#–B–D–F, vii°7 in A minor. Also called the fully diminished seventh chord. Its four notes divide the octave into equal parts, so each inversion sounds the same as another diminished seventh chord in root position.

figure.caption: vii°7 in A minor, built on the raised seventh degree.

entry.gloss: seventh chord on the seventh degree
entry.def: The seventh chord built on the leading tone: half-diminished in major (viiø7) and fully diminished in minor (vii°7), where it uses the raised seventh degree. It has dominant function and resolves to the tonic triad. Called the leading-note seventh in British English.

figure.caption: viiø7 to I in C major, then vii°7 to i in A minor.

entry.gloss: seventh chord on the second degree
entry.def: The seventh chord built on the supertonic: a minor seventh chord in major (ii7) and a half-diminished seventh chord in minor (iiø7). It is the most common predominant seventh chord, often in first inversion (ii6/5) before V.

figure.staff: [D4 F4 A4 C5]/h{ii7} [D4 F4 Ab4 C5]/h{iiø7}
figure.caption: ii7 in C major and iiø7 in C minor.

entry.gloss: chord note a seventh above the root
entry.def: The note of a seventh chord a seventh above its root: F in G–B–D–F. It is a dissonance and normally resolves down by step; in strict style it is also prepared, held over as a common tone from the chord before.

figure.caption: The seventh, F, falls to E while the leading tone rises to C.

entry.gloss: numbers that show which chord note is in the bass
entry.def: The figures from figured bass that Roman numeral analysis uses to show a chord's position. Triads: none (5/3) in root position, 6 in first inversion and 6/4 in second inversion. Seventh chords: 7 in root position, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2 in first, second and third inversion.

figure.caption: The dominant seventh of C major in root position and its three inversions.

entry.gloss: figure for a first-inversion seventh chord
entry.def: A seventh chord in first inversion, with its third in the bass, named after the sixth and fifth above the bass that mark it, 6/5: V6/5 in C major has B in the bass.

entry.gloss: figure for a second-inversion seventh chord
entry.def: A seventh chord in second inversion, with its fifth in the bass, named after the fourth and third above the bass that mark it, 4/3 (in full 6/4/3): V4/3 in C major has D in the bass.

entry.gloss: figure for a third-inversion seventh chord
entry.def: A seventh chord in third inversion, with its seventh in the bass, named after the fourth and second above the bass that mark it, 4/2 (in full 6/4/2; sometimes just 2). Because the seventh falls by step, V4/2 normally resolves to I6.

entry.gloss: seventh chord with its seventh in the bass
entry.def: A seventh chord is in third inversion when its seventh is the lowest note. Only seventh chords and larger chords have a third inversion; it is marked 4/2.

figure.caption: G–B–D–F with F in the bass.

entry.gloss: chord with one of its notes left out
entry.def: A chord with one of its notes missing. In four-part writing the fifth is the note normally left out, and another note, usually the root, is doubled: an incomplete V7 has two roots, a third and a seventh. The third and the seventh are not omitted, since they give the chord its quality.

figure.caption: V7 in C major without its fifth, D.

entry.gloss: a chord's role: tonic, predominant or dominant
entry.def: The role a chord plays in a key, which groups chords into three families: tonic (stability), predominant (moving away) and dominant (tension that leads back to the tonic). The typical phrase moves tonic – predominant – dominant – tonic. Some theorists, following Riemann, call the predominant the subdominant function.

figure.caption: Tonic, predominant, dominant and tonic again.

entry.gloss: stability and arrival: I and its substitutes
entry.def: The function of rest and arrival, held by the tonic triad, I or i. The vi chord, and in some analyses iii, can stand in for the tonic because they share two of its notes, as in the deceptive cadence.

entry.gloss: chords that lead to the dominant: ii and IV
entry.def: The function of chords that lead to the dominant, mainly ii and IV (ii° and iv in minor), with or without sevenths, in root position or first inversion. They usually contain the fourth scale degree. Also spelled pre-dominant; also called subdominant function.

figure.caption: IV and ii6 leading to V in C major.

entry.gloss: tension that leads to the tonic: V and vii°
entry.def: The function of chords that pull back to the tonic: V, V7 and the leading-tone chords vii° and vii°7 (viiø7 in major). All contain the leading tone, which needs the raised seventh degree in minor.

entry.gloss: I, IV and V
entry.def: The triads on the tonic, subdominant and dominant: I, IV and V (in minor i, iv and V). Between them they contain every note of the scale and represent the three functions, so they can harmonize most simple melodies.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/h{I} [F4 A4 C5]/h{IV} [G4 B4 D5]/h{V}

entry.gloss: ii, iii, vi and vii°
entry.def: The diatonic triads other than the primary triads: ii, iii, vi and vii° in major. Each shares two notes with a primary triad and can often take its place. Not to be confused with secondary dominants, which are chromatic chords.

figure.staff: [D4 F4 A4]/q{ii} [E4 G4 B4]/q{iii} [A4 C5 E5]/q{vi} [B4 D5 F5]/q{vii°}

entry.gloss: a series of chords moving with direction
entry.def: A series of chords heard as moving towards a goal, usually following the normal order of functions: tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic. More generally, any succession of chords.

entry.gloss: chords moving against the usual order
entry.def: A chord succession that reverses the usual order of functions, such as V–IV or V–ii, dominant to predominant. Retrogressions are less common than progressions but not wrong, especially inside a phrase.

entry.gloss: chord roots falling by fifths
entry.def: A progression whose roots fall by fifths (or rise by fourths), as on the circle of fifths: vi–ii–V–I. Falling fifths are usually considered the strongest root movement in tonal music.

entry.gloss: the interval between successive chord roots
entry.def: The interval from the root of one chord to the root of the next, whatever the chords' inversions. Roots falling by fifth, falling by third and rising by step are considered the strongest movements and are the most common, together with roots rising by fifth, as in I–V and IV–I; roots falling by step or rising by third are less common.

entry.gloss: how often the chords change
entry.def: The rhythm of the chord changes, as distinct from the rhythm of the melody. Harmonic rhythm often speeds up towards a cadence, and chord changes usually fall on strong beats.

figure.staff: E5/q D5/q C5/q E5/q | F5/q A5/q G5/q F5/q | E5/q D5/q C5/h |.
figure.caption: The melody moves in quarter notes; the harmony changes once in the first and last bars and twice in the second.

entry.gloss: harmonic and melodic close of a phrase
entry.def: A point of arrival that ends a phrase, made by a typical chord pattern and melody. Cadences ending on the tonic (authentic, plagal) sound closed; those ending on the dominant (half cadence) or replacing the expected tonic (deceptive) sound open.

entry.gloss: dominant to tonic at a phrase end
entry.def: A cadence from the dominant, V or V7, to the tonic, I or i: the strongest close in tonal music. It is either perfect or imperfect. British books call V–I a perfect cadence whatever the voicing.

entry.gloss: V–I in root position, tonic in the top voice
entry.def: An authentic cadence with both chords in root position and the tonic in the highest voice on the final chord: the most conclusive cadence. Abbreviated PAC.

figure.caption: The leading tone rises to the tonic in the soprano while the bass moves from the dominant to the tonic.

entry.gloss: V–I ending with the third or fifth on top
entry.def: An authentic cadence weaker than a perfect one. In the narrower definition, used by Caplin among others, it is root-position V–I with the third or fifth of the tonic in the highest voice; others, such as Kostka and Payne, count every authentic cadence that is not perfect, including those with an inverted chord or with vii° in place of V. Abbreviated IAC. Not the British imperfect cadence, which is a half cadence.

figure.caption: The soprano ends on the third of the tonic triad.

entry.gloss: phrase ending on V
entry.def: A cadence that ends on the dominant triad, V, usually in root position, approached from any chord, most often I, ii or IV. It sounds open, like a question. Called an imperfect cadence in British English. Abbreviated HC.

entry.gloss: IV to I: the Amen cadence
entry.def: The progression IV–I (iv–i in minor), familiar as the Amen at the end of hymns. Many theorists, Caplin among them, regard IV–I in Classical music as a prolongation of the tonic that follows an authentic cadence rather than as a phrase-ending cadence of its own.

entry.gloss: V moving to vi instead of I
entry.def: A cadence in which V moves to a chord other than the expected tonic, usually vi (VI in minor). The leading tone still rises to the tonic, which is then doubled as the third of vi. Called an interrupted cadence in British English.

entry.gloss: iv6 to V in minor
entry.def: A half cadence in minor from iv6 to V, in which the bass falls a half step from the sixth to the fifth degree while an upper voice rises a whole step to the octave. The falling half step recalls the close of the Phrygian mode.

figure.caption: In A minor: the bass falls from F to E as the soprano rises from D to E.

entry.gloss: 6/4 over the dominant bass, resolving to V
entry.def: A second-inversion tonic triad on a strong beat over the dominant in the bass, whose sixth and fourth fall by step to the fifth and third of V. Because it decorates V, books label it differently: I6/4–V, V6/4–5/3 or Cad6/4.

entry.gloss: major tonic triad ending a minor-key piece
entry.def: A major tonic triad at the end of a piece or section in a minor key, made by raising the third of the tonic: a minor-key piece in A ends on A–C#–E. Common in music of the Renaissance and Baroque.

entry.gloss: bass line with figures for the harmony
entry.def: A bass line with numbers, the figures, that show the intervals to be played above each bass note, from which a keyboard or lute player improvises the harmony. It was the standard accompaniment of the Baroque era (about 1600–1750) and is still used to teach harmony.

entry.gloss: numbers for the intervals above a bass note
entry.def: The numbers and accidentals of a figured bass, written under or over the bass notes. Each number is an interval above the bass, reckoned in the key signature and without octaves; a bass note without figures means a root-position triad (5/3), and the figures are often abbreviated, as 6 for 6/3.

entry.gloss: sharp, flat or natural that alters a figured interval
entry.def: A sharp, flat or natural in a figured bass. Next to a number it alters that interval above the bass; standing alone it alters the third. A slash through a number, as in a crossed 6, means the interval is raised.

figure.caption: In A minor, the sharp under E asks for the third above it raised to G#.

entry.gloss: chords played or written out from a figured bass
entry.def: The chords and voices that a performer improvises, or a student writes out, above a figured bass. A good realization follows the rules of voice leading. Spelled realisation in British English.

entry.gloss: Baroque bass part and the players who perform it
entry.def: The accompanying part of Baroque music, notated as a figured bass and played by a bass instrument such as a cello, viola da gamba or bassoon together with a chord instrument such as a harpsichord, organ or lute that fills in the harmony. Often shortened to continuo.

entry.gloss: the art of playing from a figured bass
entry.def: An English name for the basso continuo, a bass that runs through the whole piece (thorough is an old form of through). Like the German Generalbass, it also names the practice and teaching of playing harmony from a figured bass.
